planting.note: Drill into a firm, shallow seedbed as early as the ground can be worked in spring; Suneson is a public spring-type release meant for short-season northern rotations and tolerates light frost as a seedling.

directions: Drill Suneson at a shallow 0.25-0.5 inch depth into a firm seedbed as soon as soil is workable in early spring, since it germinates in near-freezing conditions and establishes fastest with good seed-to-soil contact. Released as a public spring camelina line by Montana State University and USDA-ARS breeding work, it is a mid-season, average-yield selection prized for a higher oil percentage and elevated alpha-linolenic acid content compared to newer sister release 'Blaine Creek', making it a reliable choice where oil quality for biodiesel or omega-3 feed use matters as much as yield. As a rotational cover between small grains, its rapid canopy closure suppresses spring weeds on marginal or drought-prone ground, and its shallow-fibrous-to-taproot system leaves soil structure intact for the following crop. Swath or direct-combine when the lower pods turn tan, and consider it primarily for northern Plains and Intermountain West rotations with cold, short growing seasons.
sources: Montana State University Extension - Camelina Variety Development
USDA Agricultural Research Service - Camelina Breeding Program
Purdue University New Crops Resource - Camelina sativa

planting.note: Drill shallowly in earliest spring as ground becomes workable; Blaine Creek is a short-season, high-yield public spring release bred for quick turnaround ahead of a following crop.

directions: Sow Blaine Creek at a shallow depth into a firm, cool seedbed as early in spring as fields can be entered, taking advantage of its ability to germinate at near-freezing soil temperatures. Bred and publicly released by Montana State University as a companion line to 'Suneson', Blaine Creek is distinguished by an especially short season to maturity and high yield potential in favorable environments, along with elevated omega-3 (alpha-linolenic) fatty acid content in the seed oil. This fast turnaround makes it a strong fit for tight double-crop or relay windows in dryland small-grain rotations across the northern Plains and Intermountain West, where a quick oilseed cover can be established, matured, and harvested before a summer crop is planted. Its dense, fast-closing canopy chokes out early spring weeds on lean or eroded ground, and stubble left after combining protects soil through the following season. Harvest by swathing or straight combining once the majority of pods have dried to a tan color.
sources: Montana State University Extension - Camelina Variety Development
USDA Agricultural Research Service - Camelina Breeding Program
Oregon State University Extension - Camelina Production Guide

planting.note: Sow direct in spring into scarified, inoculated seed on lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil; Penngift is the classic named selection bred specifically for holding steep, dry cut-and-fill slopes.

directions: Broadcast scarified, Rhizobium-inoculated 'Penngift' seed onto a roughened, lean slope in spring, then mulch or track the seed in to hold it against wash until germination; Penngift was released by Pennsylvania State University in 1953 from H. Burton Musser and Fred Grau's roadside erosion-control breeding work and remains the standard named crown vetch cultivar used by state highway and conservation agencies. Its dense, sprawling rhizomatous mats knit together loose fill and cut-slope soil far faster than the unselected wild ecotype, while its Rhizobium symbiosis builds fertility on subsoil too poor for most other legumes. Because it spreads aggressively and persists indefinitely, reserve Penngift for permanent, high-disturbance sites such as highway banks, pipeline right-of-ways, and quarry reclamation rather than rotational cropland, and never plant it near natural areas since it has escaped and become invasive across much of the eastern and midwestern US. Mow once a year after flowering to control woody encroachment; it needs no reseeding once established.
sources: Pennsylvania State University - Crown Vetch Breeding History
USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service Plant Guide - Coronilla varia
Ernst Conservation Seeds - Penngift Crownvetch

planting.note: Sow seed-in-pod in early spring on well-drained, calcareous soil; Shoshone was bred specifically for root-knot nematode tolerance and performs well on irrigated dryland ground in the Intermountain West.

directions: Drill 'Shoshone' seed-in-pod at 25-40 lb per acre in early spring into a firm, well-drained, calcareous seedbed, since this cultivar shares sainfoin's intolerance of acidic or waterlogged ground. Jointly released in 2005 by the University of Wyoming, Montana State University, and USDA-NRCS, Shoshone was selected from surviving plants in an irrigated variety trial that had been heavily infested with northern root-knot nematode, giving it markedly better persistence than older sainfoin sources on nematode-prone irrigated fields in the Mountain West. Like other sainfoins it fixes nitrogen without causing bloat in grazing livestock, and its deep taproot breaks up compacted subsoil while scavenging moisture and nutrients other legumes can't reach. Use it as a long-lived perennial soil builder in dryland or limited-irrigation rotations on chalky or calcareous ground where clover and alfalfa struggle with nematode pressure; it typically persists productively for four to six years before needing renovation.
sources: University of Wyoming / Montana State University - Release Notice of 'Shoshone' Sainfoin
USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service - Plant Materials Program
Montana State University Extension - Sainfoin Production

planting.note: Sow seed-in-pod in early spring on well-drained, calcareous soil; Remont was selected from Iranian source material for unusually rapid regrowth after cutting or grazing.

directions: Broadcast or drill 'Remont' seed-in-pod at 25-40 lb per acre into a well-drained, neutral-to-alkaline, calcareous seedbed in early spring, since like all sainfoin it fails on acidic or heavy, poorly drained soils. Released by the Montana Agricultural Experiment Station in 1971 from plant introductions collected in Iran, Remont was the first sainfoin cultivar bred specifically for rapid regrowth after cutting, enabling more than one hay or cover-crop cut per season in favorable years rather than the single-cut pattern typical of older sainfoin sources. Its deep taproot fixes nitrogen through Rhizobium symbiosis, mines subsoil moisture and minerals, and provides tannin-containing, non-bloating forage value if grazed or hayed between cover-crop cycles. Remont has since been largely superseded in irrigated multi-cut systems by the newer 'Delaney' release, but it remains a solid, widely available choice for dryland soil-building on thin, calcareous ground in the Northern Rockies and High Plains.
sources: Montana Agricultural Experiment Station - Sainfoin Variety Development
USDA NRCS Plant Guide - Onobrychis viciifolia
Agronomy Journal - An insight into sainfoin (Onobrychis viciifolia) breeding: challenges and achievements

planting.note: Sow direct in fall as temperatures cool; Charano is an early-maturing, upright yellow serradella selection bred for cleaner mechanical seed harvest than older prostrate serradella lines.

directions: Broadcast Rhizobium-inoculated 'Charano' seed at 8-12 lb per acre onto a firm, weed-free seedbed in fall, since like all serradella it nodulates poorly without an Ornithopus-specific inoculant strain. Charano was developed from a yellow serradella ecotype collected on the Greek island of Mykonos and selected for a more upright growth habit than older cultivars such as 'Paros', making standing pods far easier to header-harvest for seed while retaining similar or slightly better field performance. It thrives on the same sandy, acidic, low-fertility soils where clovers and vetches struggle, building nitrogen and organic matter through winter and spring growth before dying back with summer heat. Mow or graze off before pod shatter if reseeding is not wanted, or let pods ripen and shatter naturally in orchard, vineyard, or pasture-cropping systems for a self-renewing stand the following season.
sources: Centre for Legumes in Mediterranean Agriculture, University of Western Australia - Pasture Legume Cultivars
NSW Department of Primary Industries - Yellow Serradella
Crop & Pasture Science - Prospects for diversifying temperate pasture systems with serradella

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for a winter nitrogen-fixing cover; Paraggio is a broadly-adapted, mid-season barrel medic with a lower hard-seed level, suited to shorter rotation windows than harder-seeded medics.

directions: Broadcast or drill 'Paraggio' onto a prepared, well-drained, neutral-to-alkaline seedbed in early fall so plants establish before winter cooling, using fresh Rhizobium meliloti inoculant if the field has no recent medic history. Paraggio is a mid-season-maturing barrel medic developed for broad climatic adaptation and, notably, a lower proportion of hard (dormant) seed than older barrel medic lines, which means a greater share of the seed bank germinates the following autumn rather than remaining dormant for years, a real advantage in shorter, more intensively rotated cover-crop or ley-farming systems rather than long, continuous pasture phases. Its low, spreading annual growth fixes nitrogen for the following warm-season crop while its spiny, coiled seed pods still provide some persistence through residual hard seed. Allow at least a portion of the stand to set seed before terminating by mowing, grazing, or light incorporation in late spring, so the self-regenerating seed bank carries the cover into subsequent seasons.
sources: NSW Department of Primary Industries - Barrel Medic
Synergy Seeds - Paraggio Barrel Medic Technical Sheet
UC SAREP Cover Crop Database - Barrel Medic

planting.note: Direct sow in fall; Caliph is an early-to-mid maturing barrel medic bred for outstanding seed set, giving it strong self-regeneration for repeated cover-crop or ley-farming cycles.

directions: Broadcast 'Caliph' onto a firm, well-drained, alkaline-to-neutral seedbed in early fall with fresh medic-specific Rhizobium inoculant, allowing the low rosette to establish before cool weather sets in. Caliph is an early-to-mid maturing barrel medic, typically flowering around 80 days after germination, and is distinguished by outstanding pod and seed production that in regional trials has consistently outyielded older cultivars such as 'Parabinga' in seed set across most test sites. That heavy seed output translates directly into a dense, persistent soil seed bank, making Caliph a strong choice where growers want a self-reseeding winter legume cover that returns reliably year after year with no replanting. As with other barrel medics, its spiny, coiled pods historically clung to grazing animals for dispersal, and mature stands fix substantial nitrogen for the warm-season crop that follows. Terminate by grazing, mowing, or light tillage after a portion of pods have matured and dropped seed, timing termination to leave enough hard seed in the soil to regenerate the following autumn.
sources: Synergy Seeds - Caliph Barrel Medic Technical Sheet
Naracoorte Seeds - Caliph Barrel Medic
UC SAREP Cover Crop Database - Barrel Medic
